notable_claims: The Electronic Communications Privacy Act (ECPA) may limit what system administrators can do when searching user files.
Resource-based network restrictions applied equally to all users are framed as non-censorship issues.
Use of online handles is compared to a request to withhold a name in a letter to the editor.
classification.summary: This is a digest abstract summarizing twelve items related to digital privacy, censorship, and legal boundaries in computing. Key topics include the use of online handles for anonymity, the legality of system administrators searching user files under the ECPA, and the banning of specific newsgroups based on content.
classification.title: Abstract of CAF-News 02.28

notable_claims: The court found that artistic expression is at the core of a democratic society's cultural and political vitality, comparable to academic speech.
classification.summary: A federal judge ruled that the National Endowment for the Arts (NEA) 'decency clause' was unconstitutional due to being too vague and overbroad. The ruling emphasized that artistic expression is as central to a democratic society as academic speech or journalism. This followed a legal challenge by four artists whose grants were denied based on political and decency standards.
classification.title: Federal judge rules NEA decency clause unconstitutional

identity.subject: Article 2--[UPI] Federal judge rules NEA decency clause unconstitutional

notable_claims: University administrations are more likely to 'pull the plug' on services due to public perception of spending public money on objectionable content than police are to overreact.
Canadian courts have no jurisdiction to prosecute US publishers for illegal material.
classification.summary: Chris Lewis discusses the intersection of Canadian law, police investigations, and USENET distribution. He argues that university administrations are more likely to censor content due to public pressure and funding concerns than the police are. The post also addresses jurisdictional limits regarding the prosecution of foreign publishers for illegal material.
classification.title: Article 4--Re: Anonymous Contact Service @ wizvax

notable_claims: The US government is ethically inconsistent for denying entry to a foreigner based on their views while claiming to protect free speech.
Denying physical entry does not equate to denying the right to express ideas if the author's books are available in bookstores.
classification.summary: A Usenet discussion regarding the denial of entry into the United States for Canadian author Farley Mowat. Participants debate whether restricting a foreigner's physical entry to the country constitutes a violation of free speech principles if their written works remain available for purchase.

notable_claims: Government rests on the consent of the people and must protect a core of personal rights.
Protection for the rights of expression, conscience, speech, and belief is a minimum requirement for a legal system.
classification.summary: Mark P. Neely shares an excerpt from a speech by US Supreme Court Justice Anthony M. Kennedy regarding the philosophical foundations of the legal system. The text emphasizes the role of government consent, the protection of human rights—specifically expression and speech—and the obligation to obey the law. It serves as a theoretical framework for discussions on rights within the CAF community.

notable_claims: System administrators may be able to search their own systems without a warrant, but law enforcement requires one for evidence admissibility in court.
Publishing system rules regarding the execution of arbitrary executables can mitigate user claims of an expectation of privacy.
Administrative searches may still conflict with the ECPA or the Educational Records Privacy Act (Buckley Amendment).
classification.summary: A discussion between system administrators regarding the ethics and legality of searching user accounts for malicious software. One contributor describes using 'strings' on binaries and archiving files to prevent users from altering evidence, while another discusses the legal distinction between administrative searches and law enforcement warrants under US law.
classification.title: Legalities and policies for searching user accounts

notable_claims: NNTP accounted for 9.268% of NSFNet backbone packets in April 1992.
IRC accounted for 1.901% of NSFNet backbone packets in April 1992.
Technical restrictions applied equally to all users for load management are not necessarily censorship.
classification.summary: Wes Morgan responds to reports of network traffic restrictions at Duke University, specifically regarding IRC and gaming packets. He argues that equal application of technical restrictions for network load management does not constitute censorship. To support this, he provides NSFNet backbone statistics from April 1992 to analyze the actual impact of NNTP and IRC on network resources.

notable_claims: Repeated unwanted email can constitute harassment.
Harassment by computer is legally considered harassment.
Public newsgroup articles that offend a user are generally not classified as harassment.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie provides advice on dealing with computer-based harassment, distinguishing between private unwanted communications and public newsgroup posts. He suggests documenting the harassment, notifying administrators, and using email filters. The post includes references to legal precedents regarding email harassment and university censorship policies.
